text: Washington
Texas confirmed. Now Washington — and I want to check My Health My Data, which is one of the very few other private rights of action.
MHMDA creates
a private right of action, though there's a critical distinction around what counts as "consumer health data." The statute
explicitly lists biometric data as a category, but the real question is whether biometrics used solely for identity verification—rather than to infer health information—fall
within that definition. The definition itself ties consumer health data to personal information linked or reasonably linkable to a consumer's
health status, which creates ambiguity about purely identity-focused biometric uses.
Washington
's statute has two critical advantages: it explicitly excludes data generated from photographs—unlike Illinois—which
means face scans derived from camera images likely fall outside the law entirely. Plus, the "security purpose" definition directly covers identity verification at signup since it
includes fraud prevention and protecting account integrity.
Two strong Washington find
ings — the statute's photo carve-out and the "security purpose" exemption both likely cut in our favour. Recording Texas + Washington.

text: Done. Here's what I found

and what's waiting for you.

## The headline

**Illinois is the only genuinely dangerous state to launch in.** Everything else is either manageable compliance work or attorney-general risk you

reduce by doing what Illinois already forces you to do.

Three findings that I think change your plan:

**1. The BIPA amendment everyone celebrated doesn't help

you.** SB 2979 (2024) killed per-scan damages, and the Seventh Circuit made it retroactive in April 2026. But per-scan only ever mattered for employee timeclocks scanning 1,000+ times a year. You scan once at signup —

so your exposure was always ~1x per user and still is: **$1,000–$5,000 per Illinois user**, plus plaintiffs' fees, actionable for five years. Most summaries of that amendment would have led you to the wrong conclusion on

your own facts.

**2. You may be exempt from BIPA entirely.** §14/25(c) exempts GLBA-covered financial institutions, and GLBA reaches further than "bank." I made this

the first subtask because the answer reorders everything else. The catch: in *Davis v. Jumio* the exemption didn't protect the verification vendor — so it may cover you while leaving your vendor exposed, which makes their indemnity clause the thing to read clos

ely.

**3. The brief was missing a regime.** "Monthly subscription" triggers auto-renewal law independently of biometrics, and one requirement is a product change rather than a policy document: **New York requires a cancel button inside the mobile app**, and Color

ado has required one-step online cancellation since February 2026. Worth saying the FTC's click-to-cancel rule was vacated in July 2025 and isn't binding right now — but rulemaking restarted in January

2026 and the replacement is expected to look much like the original, so building to it now is free.

## Two pleasant surprises

Washington's biometric statute probably doesn't reach you at all —

it excludes data *generated from* photographs (the opposite result to Illinois on identical facts) and has a fraud/security-purpose exemption that fits signup verification neatly. NYC and Portland are both drafted around physical premises, so a p

ure app likely escapes both.

## Two things I didn't decide for you

Whether you're GLBA-covered, and whether Washington's My Health My Data Act treats identity-verification biometrics as "consumer health data." The second is genuinely unsettled — it's the only other private right of

action in the country, so I flagged it for counsel rather than guessing.

## One note on sequencing

The biometric statutes (IL/TX/WA) have **no size threshold** and bind you from user #1. The ~22 comprehensive privacy laws

mostly don't bite until ~100k in-state users, Maryland lowest at 35k. So if someone pitches a 22-state privacy programme as the launch blocker, that's the wrong order.

**Cheapest high-value

fix in the tree:** delete the face template the instant the match succeeds. Retention past verification is the most commonly pleaded violation and the hardest to defend, because your own stated purpose is complete by then.
